name: Isaiah
author: Isaiah son of Amoz was a prophet in Jerusalem, active for about forty years, from around 740 to 700 BC, under Kings Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz and Hezekiah. He moved in royal circles and spoke directly to kings. He was married, and he gave his sons names that carried messages. Tradition credits him with the whole book; many scholars think chapters 40–66 were added by later prophets in his tradition, writing during and after the exile in Babylon.
audience: The first hearers were the people of Jerusalem and Judah, including their kings and leaders. They lived under constant threat from Assyria and were tempted to trust in foreign alliances. Chapters 40–66 speak to a later situation: Jews exiled in Babylon after Jerusalem's destruction, and then those returning to rebuild a ruined city.
era: Isaiah lived as Assyria, a ruthless empire based in what is now northern Iraq, pushed west. In 722 BC Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel, and in 701 BC its king Sennacherib overran Judah and besieged Jerusalem. Judah's kings wavered between submitting to Assyria and seeking help from Egypt. The later chapters look to Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BC, the exile that followed, and the rise of Cyrus of Persia, who let the exiles return from 538 BC.

notes.1:2: Many scholars link this picture of a land overrun and Jerusalem left isolated to the Assyrian invasion of Judah in 701 BC.
notes.2:1: An almost identical passage appears in Micah, a prophet working in Judah at the same time; scholars debate who borrowed from whom, or whether both drew on an older source.
notes.6:1: This vision is set in the Jerusalem temple and dated to the year King Uzziah died, around 740 BC, after his long reign of about fifty years.
notes.7:1: Around 735 BC the kings of Aram (Syria) and northern Israel marched on Jerusalem to force King Ahaz to join their alliance against Assyria.
notes.8:1: This passage comes from the same crisis; Assyria went on to capture Damascus in 732 BC and Samaria in 722 BC.
notes.8:16: Zebulun and Naphtali, in Galilee in the far north, were among the first areas Assyria took from Israel, around 732 BC.
notes.9:8: This section is aimed at the northern kingdom of Israel, also called Ephraim, whose capital was Samaria, in the years before Assyria destroyed it in 722 BC.
notes.10:5: The cities listed, such as Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad and Damascus, all fell to Assyria's armies during the decades of Isaiah's ministry.
notes.10:28: The towns named trace an army's march from the north toward Jerusalem, ending at Nob, a hill within sight of the city.
notes.11:1: Jesse was the father of King David, so this passage looks to David's royal family, which still ruled Judah in Isaiah's day.
notes.13:1: This oracle concerns Babylon; some scholars place it in Isaiah's day, when Babylon was resisting Assyria, while many date it later, when Babylon itself ruled the region.
notes.14:28: This oracle is dated to the year King Ahaz died, around 727 or 715 BC (scholars differ on which), and addressed to Philistia, Judah's neighbour on the Mediterranean coast.
notes.15:1: Moab was a kingdom east of the Dead Sea, a close neighbour and frequent rival of Israel and Judah; the many towns named were Moabite cities.
notes.17:1: Damascus was the capital of Aram, roughly modern Syria, which was allied with northern Israel against Judah; Assyria captured it in 732 BC.
notes.18:1: Cush was the land south of Egypt, roughly modern Sudan, whose kings ruled Egypt in this period and sent envoys seeking allies against Assyria.
notes.19:1: Egypt was Judah's powerful southern neighbour, and many in Jerusalem looked to it for protection against Assyria.
notes.20:1: This is dated to around 711 BC, when Sargon of Assyria sent his commander to capture Ashdod, a Philistine city that had rebelled hoping for Egyptian help.
notes.21:1: The 'wilderness of the sea' refers to southern Babylonia; scholars debate whether this fall of Babylon happened in Isaiah's lifetime or is Persia's conquest of 539 BC.
notes.21:11: Dumah was an oasis in northern Arabia, and Seir is another name for Edom, the land south-east of the Dead Sea.
notes.21:13: Dedan, Tema and Kedar were desert tribes and trading oases of northern Arabia, known for their camel caravans.
notes.22:1: The 'Valley of Vision' refers to Jerusalem; the strengthening of walls and storing of water are widely linked to Hezekiah's preparations for the Assyrian siege around 701 BC.
notes.22:15: Shebna was the senior official in charge of the royal palace; an ancient tomb inscription found near Jerusalem may belong to him.
notes.23:1: Tyre and Sidon were wealthy Phoenician port cities on the coast of modern Lebanon, famous for sea trade across the Mediterranean.
notes.24:1: Chapters 24–27 are often called the 'Isaiah Apocalypse'; scholars debate their date, with suggestions ranging from Isaiah's own time to well after the exile.
notes.28:1: This is addressed first to Samaria, capital of the northern kingdom, before its fall to Assyria in 722 BC.
notes.28:14: The 'covenant with death' is widely thought to refer to the Jerusalem leaders' alliance with Egypt against Assyria during Hezekiah's reign.
notes.29:1: 'Ariel' is a poetic name for Jerusalem, the city where King David had set up his camp.
notes.30:1: Judah's leaders were sending envoys to Egypt, to cities such as Zoan, seeking an alliance against Assyria, probably in the years before 701 BC.
notes.34:1: Edom, south-east of the Dead Sea, was Judah's neighbour and long-standing rival; Bozrah was one of its chief cities.
notes.36:1: This is dated to Hezekiah's fourteenth year, 701 BC, when Sennacherib of Assyria invaded Judah; much the same account appears in 2 Kings 18–19.
notes.38:9: The heading presents this poem as written by King Hezekiah himself after he recovered from his illness.
notes.39:1: Merodach-baladan was a Babylonian leader who repeatedly rebelled against Assyria; his envoys were likely seeking Judah's support.
notes.40:1: Many scholars think chapters 40–66 were written for Jews exiled in Babylon around 550–540 BC; the traditional view is that Isaiah foresaw that time.
notes.41:1: The conqueror stirred up from the east is widely identified as Cyrus, the Persian king whose armies were sweeping across the region.
notes.42:1: This is the first of four passages scholars call the 'Servant Songs', which centre on a figure called the Lord's servant.
notes.44:24: Cyrus is named here: the Persian king who captured Babylon in 539 BC and allowed exiled Jews to return home.
notes.46:1: Bel and Nebo were leading gods of Babylon, whose statues were carried through the city in great religious processions.
notes.47:1: Babylon was famous for its astrologers and stargazers, whom its kings consulted to read the future.
notes.52:13: This is the last and longest of the four 'Servant Songs'.
notes.56:1: Many scholars link chapters 56–66 to the years after exiles began returning to Jerusalem in 538 BC; others keep them with Isaiah's own work.
notes.63:1: Bozrah was a chief city of Edom, Judah's south-eastern neighbour and old rival.
notes.63:15: The burned temple and ruined cities described here are widely linked to Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem in 587 BC.
notes.66:1: Many scholars connect this passage to the period of rebuilding the temple, which was finished around 515 BC.

flags.problem: States as settled fact that chapters 40–66 address exiles in Babylon and returnees. That is the scholarly view. In the traditional view, Isaiah himself wrote these chapters, foreseeing that time, so the original hearers were still his own people. The author section and the 40:1 note handle this fairly, but here it reads as fact.
flags.suggestion: Hedge it, e.g. 'Many scholars think chapters 40–66 were written for a later situation… ; traditionally they are read as Isaiah's words looking ahead to that time.'

flags.problem: Calls the section the 'Isaiah Apocalypse' without explaining 'apocalypse'. Ordinary readers may take it to mean simply 'disaster' or 'the end of the world'.
flags.suggestion: Add a short gloss, e.g. 'often called the "Isaiah Apocalypse" because, like the book of Revelation, they describe judgment and renewal on a worldwide scale.'

unsure.problem: Zebulun and Naphtali are not named until 9:1 in English Bibles (8:23 in Hebrew). A reader tapping 8:16 gets a note about places that do not appear for several verses, which may confuse.
unsure.suggestion: Restored: notes cannot move. Word it for its passage. Original suggestion: Move this note to 9:1, or give 8:16 a note about the passage it actually opens.
